citation: Morel, G. M. (2021). Student-centered learning: context needed. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-021-09951-0
title: Own It, Learn It, Share It framework for student-centered learning
description: Lee and Hannafin's design framework "intersects constructivist, constructionist, and self-determination theories to address student-centered learning." It has three parts: "Own It involves students developing ownership over the process and achieving personally meaningful learning goals," Learn It involves autonomous learning "through metacognitive, procedural, conceptual, and strategic scaffolding," and Share It involves students generating "artifacts aimed at authentic audiences beyond the classroom assessment." The framework also includes "ten discrete design guidelines for the instructional design process."
requirements: The framework is described as combining constructivist, constructionist, and self-determination theories
constraints: Cheng notes it is a time-consuming, general approach rather than an efficient, customizable approach in times of restricted resources
target_learners: students in digital and online learning contexts
examples: Baird applied the framework as a blueprint to a flexible assignment designed to promote intrinsic motivation and engagement

article_title: Response to “A design framework for enhancing engagement in student-centered learning: own it, learn it, and share it”: a design perspective
citation: Xiaoqing Gu. (2021). Response to “A design framework for enhancing engagement in student-centered learning: own it, learn it, and share it”: a design perspective. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09896-w
title: Lee and Hannafin's own it, learn it, and share it design framework for enhancing engagement in student-centered learning, revisited from a design perspective
description: This response essay revisits the design framework that Lee and Hannafin published in 2016 for "enhancing engagement in student-centered learning," which the abstract names by its three-part motto "own it, learn it, and share it." The essay discusses the framework's "value, application, and future development" in light of the pandemic-era move to full-scale online teaching. The detailed framework content appears in the underlying 2016 article rather than in the visible portion of this essay.
requirements: The essay treats the framework as applicable to student-centered learning in online teaching and learning practice, where learners own, learn, and share their learning.
constraints: The visible abstract does not print the framework's internal design details; the essay is a response commentary rather than a restatement of the framework.
target_learners: students in online and technology-supported learning environments
examples: The author revisited the 2016 Lee and Hannafin article and discussed its value, application, and future development as a response to a special issue call on shifting to digital.

article_title: Chaos: exploring an engaging online model for rapid application during the pandemic
citation: Joshua W. Tabor. (2020). Chaos: exploring an engaging online model for rapid application during the pandemic. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09878-y
title: The Own it, Learn it, Share it framework structures student-centered online learning in three steps
description: Tabor describes Lee and Hannafin's framework as a three-step student-centered course design built on self-determination theory, constructivism, and constructionism. In 'own it', students set their own goals; in 'learn it', teachers support them through direct instruction, tools, resources or discourse; in 'share it', students present a completed artifact to a selected group for feedback. Each step is designed to provide support as students explore topics interesting to them with a tangible product evaluated upon completion.
requirements: Teachers must understand the rationale behind each step of the framework, which the authors support with multiple examples explaining the 'why'
constraints: Applying the outline may be difficult due to a possible lack of understanding of student-centered learning techniques, lack of time to train teachers, and possibly teacher apathy towards online education
target_learning_goals: Student engagement and lifelong learning in digital, student-centered environments
examples: Tabor proposes schools let teachers practice with the framework and set expectations that some, if not all, of it be followed when planning for the upcoming year
key_sources: Joshua W. Tabor. (2020). Chaos: exploring an engaging online model for rapid application during the pandemic. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09878-y
